title: Kollontai and the Workers' Opposition

cards.h: The Bolshevik who argued for women's freedom
cards.b: Alexandra Kollontai (1872-1952) was a Bolshevik feminist and a leader of the Workers' Opposition in 1920-21. She argued that unions and workers, not party officials, should run industry. Her work on women, love and the family is central to Marxist feminism. Her ideas were pushed aside once Stalin took control of the state.

Born in 1872 to a St Petersburg officer's family, Kollontai joined the Social Democrats in 1899. She spent years in exile in Europe. She returned in 1917 and became People's Commissar for Social Welfare in the first Bolshevik government, a post she held until 1918. She was one of the few women at the top of the revolutionary party.

Kollontai argued that the family had to be remade, not simply reformed. Women's domestic labour, she said, should be replaced by communal kitchens, laundries and nurseries. This would free women to work and take part in public life. She saw the family as an economic unit that a socialist society must transform.

Her pamphlet The Workers' Opposition argued that the management of industry should belong to an All-Russian Congress of Producers, that is, to the unions. She opposed the growing bureaucracy of party officials. Alongside Shlyapnikov, she won a wide following among metalworkers in 1920-21. The party leadership saw the group as a threat to its control.

In Make Way for Winged Eros (1923), Kollontai argued that love in a communist society should rest on comradeship and mutual respect, not property or possession. Later writers wrongly turned her essay into the 'glass of water' theory of sex, which she never held. Her ideas on love are often misread, and they were controversial in her own day.

At the Tenth Congress in 1921 Lenin condemned the Workers' Opposition as a syndicalist and anarchist deviation. The ban on factions was passed in the same week, and it ended open debate on this line. Kollontai was left a voice without a faction. She later served as a Soviet diplomat abroad, becoming ambassador to Sweden from 1930 to 1945.

Silvia Federici's Wages Against Housework (1975) and other Marxist feminists argue that the Bolshevik model left unpaid reproductive labour hidden. Women were drawn into factories while still doing the housework. Stalin's 1936 law banned most abortions and promoted large families. For critics, the Soviet state promised equality but kept the double burden in place.

cards.h: Women workers and the Indian Left
cards.b: The Indian Left has its own women's organisations. The All India Democratic Women's Association (AIDWA), founded in 1981, took up wages, dowry deaths and violence against women. Women in trade unions, such as bidi workers and textile workers, were central to Left movements in Bengal and Kerala. Critics say the Left often treated women's issues as secondary to class, the same concern Kollontai raised in the 1920s.

Kollontai served as a diplomat in Norway (1923-30) and in Mexico (1926-27). Her posts put her outside the centre of Soviet politics, yet she kept writing on women, peace and the working class. In Sweden she worked for the Soviet case during the Second World War. She survived the purges that killed many of her comrades.

Key takeaways

  1. Kollontai was People's Commissar for Social Welfare in 1917-18.
  2. She proposed communal services to free women from housework.
  3. The Workers' Opposition wanted unions, not officials, to run industry.
  4. The Tenth Congress ban ended her faction's public role.
  5. Marxist feminists say the Soviet model left the double burden in place.

Practice question

Did the Bolshevik revolution advance women's emancipation? Answer in 200 words, citing Kollontai and the 1936 law.
